title: Powell's first Green–Colorado expedition
why_famous: The first recorded complete boat descent of the Green and Colorado canyons through the Grand Canyon by a U.S. scientific party.
route_summary: Green River, Wyoming → Green River canyons → Colorado confluence → Grand Canyon → St. Thomas, Nevada.
source_title: National Park Service — John Wesley Powell
geometry_note: Named canyon and confluence anchors trace the pre-dam river corridor. Lake Flaming Gorge, Lake Powell, and Lake Mead now obscure major reaches; interpolated lines do not recover the 1869 channel.

title: Orellana's Amazon descent
why_famous: The first recorded European voyage from the Amazon headwaters to the Atlantic, documented by expedition chronicler Gaspar de Carvajal.
route_summary: Napo/Curaray vicinity → Napo → Solimões/Amazon → Atlantic mouth.
source_title: Museo de América — Proyecto Amazonas
geometry_note: The upper Napo start, 1542 channel, island passages, and exact Atlantic outlet are uncertain. Named modern confluences provide a broad corridor only.

title: Marquette–Jolliet Mississippi journey
why_famous: Their account traced much of the Mississippi for France, building on longstanding Indigenous knowledge of its waterways.
route_summary: Lake Michigan → Fox–Wisconsin portage → Mississippi to Arkansas River vicinity → Illinois River return.
source_title: National Park Service — River of History
geometry_note: Portage and return are separate legs. River junctions are supported historically, while seventeenth-century channels and precise canoe tracks are not.

title: La Salle's Mississippi descent
why_famous: La Salle reached the Gulf of Mexico and claimed the Mississippi basin for France as Louisiana.
route_summary: Illinois River country → Mississippi → Gulf of Mexico.
source_title: National Park Service — La Salle and Louisiana
geometry_note: The river course is anchored by known confluences and settlements. Exact 1682 channels and the party's distributary through the delta are unresolved.
wiki_title: René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle

title: Fulton's North River Steamboat
why_famous: Its New York to Albany service made steam propulsion commercially credible on the Hudson River.
route_summary: New York City → Livingston estate at Clermont → Albany → return.
source_title: Smithsonian — Fulton's firsthand account
geometry_note: Documented terminals and river towns; exact 1807 ferry channel and landing at Clermont are approximate.

title: Lewis and Clark's Missouri–Columbia journey
why_famous: The federally backed expedition crossed North America to the Pacific and kept detailed journals and maps.
route_summary: St. Louis → Missouri River → continental divide portage → Clearwater, Snake, Columbia → Pacific coast.
source_title: National Park Service — Lewis and Clark journey
geometry_note: Outbound route only. River anchors trace a well documented sequence, but meanders, portages, and channel alignments are simplified.

title: Stanley's Lualaba–Congo descent
why_famous: The expedition demonstrated that the Lualaba drained west into the Congo and followed it toward the Atlantic.
route_summary: Nyangwe → Lualaba → Kisangani/Stanley Falls → middle Congo → Pool Malebo → lower Congo → Atlantic.
source_title: Library of Congress — Through the Dark Continent
geometry_note: This is a broad named-river reconstruction. Rapids, forced carries, uncertain nineteenth-century channels, and contested local place names prevent a precise track.

title: Roosevelt–Rondon River of Doubt expedition
why_famous: Roosevelt and Rondon charted a little known Amazon tributary during a dangerous downstream expedition.
route_summary: Rio da Dúvida headwaters → Rio Roosevelt → Aripuanã confluence.
source_title: Library of Congress — Roosevelt–Rondon guide
geometry_note: The upper river's exact launch and 1914 camps are not georeferenced here. Broad waypoints indicate the surveyed corridor through central Amazonia, not observed positions.

anchors.name: Aripuanã confluence
anchors.note: Modern confluence; historic river camps unresolved

title: Humboldt–Bonpland Orinoco/Casiquiare circuit
why_famous: The journey documented the natural Casiquiare water connection between the Orinoco and Amazon basins.
route_summary: Apure → Orinoco → Atabapo → Rio Negro → Casiquiare → upper Orinoco.
source_title: Humboldt digital edition — 1800 itinerary
geometry_note: The documented circuit is reconstructed at named confluences. Remote side channels and nineteenth-century river courses are approximate.

title: La Condamine's Amazon survey
why_famous: La Condamine's scientific descent produced a longitude based map of the navigable Amazon.
route_summary: Jaén/Borja → Marañón/Amazon → Pará/Belém → Atlantic transfer toward Cayenne.
source_title: Bibliothèque nationale de France — La Condamine map
geometry_note: Amazon riverway anchored by named towns and tributary junctions; eighteenth-century channels and the transfer from the Amazon mouth to Cayenne are approximate.

title: Pedro Teixeira's Amazon ascent and return
why_famous: The Portuguese expedition traversed the Amazon from Pará toward the Andes and returned, extending colonial knowledge and claims.
route_summary: Pará/Belém → Amazon → Napo → Quito region → return to Pará.
source_title: Library of Congress — Portugal country study
geometry_note: The full expedition's land route to Quito and river courses are simplified. Historic distributaries and return path are not recoverable from these city anchors.

title: Mackenzie's Arctic river journey
why_famous: Mackenzie reached the Arctic Ocean by the great northern river that later took his name.
route_summary: Fort Chipewyan → Lake Athabasca → Slave River → Great Slave Lake → Mackenzie/Dehcho → Arctic delta → return.
source_title: Smithsonian Libraries — Mackenzie and Dene account
geometry_note: Lakes, Slave River, Mackenzie/Dehcho, and return are distinct legs. Delta distributary and eighteenth-century camp positions remain uncertain.

title: David Thompson's Columbia passage
why_famous: Thompson followed the Columbia to its Pacific mouth and mapped a major transcontinental trade waterway.
route_summary: Kootenae House → Columbia → Fort Astoria; return upriver to The Dalles, then Snake/Palouse and overland via Spokane House to Kettle Falls, continuing up the Columbia.
source_title: Dictionary of Canadian Biography — David Thompson; Parks Canada route guide
geometry_note: The DCB biography describes the return route via The Dalles, up the Snake to the Palouse mouth, then by horses to Spokane House and overland to Kettle Falls before continuing upriver. The return is split by mode accordingly. House, river junction, and portage coordinates are approximate locators, not recovered 1811 survey positions; reservoirs have submerged historical reaches.

additional_sources.title: Parks Canada — David Thompson route guide
additional_sources.note: Provides regional Columbia route context; this display keeps the return's Snake/Palouse and horse-portage sequence distinct.

title: Simon Fraser's Fraser River descent
why_famous: Fraser and his party traversed the formidable canyon of the river later named for him, reaching its Pacific mouth.
route_summary: Fort George/Prince George → Fraser Canyon → Fraser Delta → return.
source_title: Parks Canada — Simon Fraser history
geometry_note: River course follows present named reaches and settlements. Historic canyon passages, tidal delta branches, and the upriver return are schematic.

title: French Mekong exploration commission
why_famous: The commission mapped the Mekong basin and showed that its cataracts frustrated hopes of a continuous trade route to China.
route_summary: Saigon → Cambodia and Mekong → Laos → Yunnan overland → Red/Yangtze rivers → Shanghai.
source_title: BnF — Mekong expedition itinerary map
geometry_note: The mission changed modes repeatedly. Lower Mekong, upper Mekong, overland Yunnan, and Yangtze legs are separated; exact 1860s channels and inland paths remain approximate.

title: Livingstone's Zambezi and Shire expedition
why_famous: The expedition surveyed the Zambezi and Shire river systems as possible routes into inland southeast Africa.
route_summary: Zambezi delta → lower Zambezi to Tete; separate Zambezi/Shire excursions and a 1859 overland walk toward Lake Nyasa (not fully geolocated).
source_title: David Livingstone — Narrative of an Expedition to the Zambesi and Its Tributaries
geometry_note: Representative partial itinerary, not one continuous vessel track. Livingstone's narrative says steamer navigation ended at Panda Mokua below Kebrabasa; the foot reconnaissance and 1859 walk toward Lake Nyasa are not geolocated here. The cataract landing (Mamvira, approx. 15°55′S) has no verified longitude, so no guessed portage or through-cataract line is drawn. Delta and lower Shire channels remain approximate.

additional_sources.title: Livingstone's 1 November 1859 letter on the Shire walk and cataracts
additional_sources.note: Contemporary letter describes the long walk and cataract reach; it does not give a mappable landing longitude.

additional_sources.title: Library of Congress — narrative map and expedition record
additional_sources.note: Institutional digitization of the expedition narrative; other Zambezi/Shire phases are not one continuous track.

anchors.name: Matope
anchors.note: Approximate lower-Shire locator; the plotted segment is schematic and not a claim of vessel passage into the cataract chain.

title: Mungo Park's final Niger expedition
why_famous: Park's attempt to follow the Niger to the sea ended at the rapids near Bussa.
route_summary: Upper Niger near Bamako → Timbuktu bend → downstream to Bussa.
source_title: Library of Congress — Nigeria country study
geometry_note: Surviving accounts establish major reaches and the Bussa endpoint but not an exact 1805–06 track. The broad Niger bend is reconstructed with modern place anchors.

title: Richard and John Lander's Niger descent
why_famous: The brothers' downstream voyage established the Niger's outlet through its delta to the Gulf of Guinea.
route_summary: Bussa → Niger → Nun River distributary → Atlantic.
source_title: Royal Geographical Society — Richard Lander
geometry_note: The river and delta route is anchored at modern towns. The nineteenth-century delta distributary and exact ocean exit are approximate.

title: Zebulon Pike's upper Mississippi reconnaissance
why_famous: Pike led an early U.S. military survey up the upper Mississippi after the Louisiana Purchase.
route_summary: St. Louis by boat → Little Falls stockade → winter sled/foot and frozen-waterway trip via Sandy, Leech and Cass Lakes → return to stockade → Mississippi by boat after thaw.
source_title: Zebulon Pike, An Account of Expeditions to the Sources of the Mississippi (1810)
geometry_note: The boats stopped near Little Falls for winter; Pike's northern journey continued by sled, foot, and frozen waterways via Lower Red Cedar, Sandy, Leech, and Upper Red Cedar (Cass) Lakes, then back by a direct cross-country route to the stockade. The party descended by boat after breakup. Lake/settlement points are modern locators; the line is not a recovered winter trail or continuous navigable river route.

additional_sources.title: Collections of the Minnesota Historical Society, vol. 7 — Pike's upper Mississippi chart
additional_sources.note: Explains Pike's Upper Red Cedar as modern Cass Lake and distinguishes Lower Red Cedar.

title: J. C. Ives's Colorado steamboat survey
why_famous: Ives's steamboat survey and subsequent land work mapped the lower Colorado and the Grand Canyon region.
route_summary: Gulf of California → Colorado River mouth → lower Colorado → Black Canyon vicinity → overland Grand Canyon survey.
source_title: Library of Congress — Ives expedition map
geometry_note: The upstream steamboat limit and land survey are separate. Lower Colorado has been heavily altered by dams and diversions; the historic channel is schematic.

title: Henry Hudson's Half Moon river ascent
why_famous: Hudson's Dutch sponsored voyage made a famous early European survey of the river later named for him.
route_summary: New York Bay → Hudson estuary → Albany vicinity → return.
source_title: National Park Service — Hudson River Valley
geometry_note: The vessel's turnaround near present Albany is historically broad; estuary channel and anchorage positions are approximate.

title: Champlain's Ottawa River journey
why_famous: Champlain's journey helped document a longstanding Indigenous travel corridor between the St. Lawrence and upper Ottawa.
route_summary: Montréal → Ottawa River → Chenaux portage and Muskrat Lake → Morrison Island near Allumette Lake.
source_title: Parks Canada — Champlain route history
geometry_note: A Parks Canada historical study traces the 1613 detour through small lakes to Muskrat Lake and Morrison Island. These lake and portage waypoints are approximate; the route follows a longstanding Indigenous waterway.

anchors.name: Chenaux reach
anchors.note: River departure for Indigenous guided bypass

title: Sultana's final Mississippi voyage
why_famous: An overloaded steamboat exploded north of Memphis in the deadliest U.S. maritime disaster.
route_summary: Vicksburg → Memphis → explosion site north of Memphis; intended Cairo/St. Louis not mapped.
source_title: National Park Service — Sultana history
geometry_note: Documented origin, Memphis stop, and explosion reach. The 1865 main channel and precise wreck location shifted over time.

title: Robert E. Lee versus Natchez steamboat race
why_famous: The New Orleans to St. Louis contest became the most celebrated Mississippi steamboat race.
route_summary: New Orleans → Baton Rouge → Natchez → Vicksburg → Memphis → St. Louis.
source_title: Library of Congress — contemporary race print
geometry_note: Race endpoints and major ports are known; routes through nineteenth-century cutoffs, bends, and the vessels' separate stops are not resolved.

title: Franklin's Coppermine River expedition
why_famous: Franklin's Arctic survey followed the Coppermine to Coronation Gulf and became notorious for its disastrous return.
route_summary: Fort Enterprise → Coppermine River → Coronation Gulf → Point Turnagain → Arctic Sound and Hood River → overland via Point Lake to Fort Enterprise.
source_title: Royal Museums Greenwich — Franklin expedition archive
geometry_note: The sea passage follows broad coastal waypoints; Point Turnagain uses the expedition's approximate plotted position. The return crossed to Hood River, then went overland via Point Lake, rather than retracing the Coppermine. Remote river, coast, and portage corridors are schematic.
